domain: Religious Studies / Comparative Religion / Japanese History
topic_summary: Analysis of Shinbutsu-shugo (Shinto-Buddhist syncretism) in Japan, examining whether 1,200 years of institutional coexistence represents a single fused ontological commitment or a pragmatic domain-partitioned bundle. The system persisted from the 6th century until forced separation in 1868, with over 90% of major shrines hosting affiliated Buddhist temples by the medieval period, yet the two traditions never fully merged and maintained distinct identities within an unsystematized relationship.

key_entities: Jingū-ji (shrine-temple complexes, institutional form of syncretism)
Tendai and Shingon sects (Buddhist movements claiming kami-buddha unity)
Meiji government (forced separation via shinbutsu bunri laws 1868+)
Kami (Shinto deities, associated with life, purity, national identity)
Buddhas (Buddhist enlightened beings, associated with death, afterlife)
Kamidana and butsudan (household shrines and altars, persistence markers)
Amaterasu Ōmikami (claimed single source in syncretic doctrines)
key_tensions: Ontological unity vs functional coexistence (did kami and buddhas fuse or merely cohabit?)
Life domain (Shinto) vs death domain (Buddhist) partition
Systematic integration (jingū-ji ubiquity) vs systematic separation (shinbutsu kakuri)
1,200-year persistence vs never achieving full fusion

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The ontological relationship between kami and buddhas — whether they are manifestations of a single ultimate reality or parallel but separate entities
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Interpretive authority distributed across Buddhist sects (Tendai, Shingon claiming unity), shrine institutions (maintaining kami autonomy), imperial court (patronizing both), and later kokugaku scholars (asserting Shinto primacy). No single adjudicator; legitimacy derived from institutional practice rather than doctrinal resolution.

readings.commitment: Kami and buddhas are manifestations of a single ultimate reality (honji suijaku doctrine: buddhas are original forms, kami are local traces)
readings.authority_grounding: Tendai and Shingon esoteric Buddhism; syncretic movements like Sannō Ichijitsu Shintō claiming Amaterasu as universal source
readings.expected_structural_delta: Institutional integration (jingū-ji ubiquity); doctrinal synthesis attempts; high ε suppression of separation discourse until Meiji

readings.commitment: Kami and buddhas govern separate domains (life/purity vs death/afterlife) without ontological unity
readings.authority_grounding: Functional practice ('born Shinto, die Buddhist'); Shinto aversion to death pollution; shinbutsu kakuri (systematic kami exclusion from Buddhism)
readings.expected_structural_delta: Compartmentalized ritual practice; life-cycle domain boundaries; persistent dual household altars (kamidana/butsudan); low ε for ontological synthesis

readings.commitment: Kami and buddhas are parallel but separate entities coexisting without fusion or domain partition
readings.authority_grounding: Historical evidence of 'difficult, largely un-systematized and tense relationship'; post-Meiji persistence of dual practice despite separation laws
readings.expected_structural_delta: Institutional coexistence without doctrinal resolution; relationship exists 'between particular kami and particular buddhas' rather than systems; functional coherence without ontological coherence

axiom_contradictions.basis: Fused ontology requires kami and buddhas to be ultimately identical (different manifestations of one reality); parallel entities reading requires them to be fundamentally distinct. No single framework can hold both that X and Y are the same thing and that X and Y are different things.

axes.primary_observable: Prevalence of syncretic doctrines (Sannō Ichijitsu Shintō, Ryōbu Shintō); jingū-ji institutional dominance (90%+ major shrines by medieval period); suppression of separation discourse pre-Meiji
axes.selection_reason: Highest institutional extractiveness; Buddhist sects gained administrative control over shrine finances and personnel via ontological synthesis claim

omegas.description: Does the 1,200-year persistence prove functional coherence sufficient for 'kernel' status, or does the failure to achieve ontological synthesis prove it was always an incoherent bundle? The three readings may collapse into 'no single kernel existed' if generation reveals they describe different phenomena rather than different interpretations of one phenomenon.
omegas.source: §1.3-K kernel/reading decomposition; user's explicit 'D2 half-break' flag

omegas.description: Was shinbutsu bunri (Meiji separation) a snare extracting shrine autonomy for state Shinto construction, or a scaffold attempting to restore a pre-syncretic 'pure' Shinto that never existed? Kokugaku influence suggests extraction; incomplete separation (stalled 1873) suggests scaffold failure.
omegas.source: Deferred axis meiji_separation_extraction; Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan)

omegas.description: Honji suijaku doctrine claimed buddhas were original forms (honji) and kami were local traces (suijaku). Did any movement reverse this (kami as original, buddhas as traces)? If so, that would be a fourth reading. Research context does not surface this; absence may be significant.

Do the three readings map to elite (doctrinal synthesis), popular (domain partition), and scholarly (parallel entities) strata? If so, the 'kernel' may be a class-stratified bundle rather than a contested ontology. Household practice (kamidana/butsudan) suggests popular domain partition; syncretic doctrines suggest elite fusion.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 1 (Operational Medium); extraction of household vs institutional practices
